result.summary: Demeter refuses all appeals from the gods, so Zeus sends Hermes to Hades to fetch Persephone. Hades lets her go but secretly gives her a pomegranate seed. Mother and daughter reunite, and Persephone tells how she was seized.

scenes.title: Demeter refuses the gods
scenes.summary: The gods offer gifts, but Demeter vows not to return to Olympus or let crops grow until she sees her daughter.
scenes.stakes: Demeter's grief over her daughter; the gods risk losing mortal offerings if the earth stays barren.

scenes.title: Hermes visits Hades
scenes.summary: Zeus sends Hermes to Erebus. Hades smiles grimly and tells Persephone to go to her mother.
scenes.stakes: Hades risks losing his wife; the gods risk ruin of their honours if Demeter's anger continues.

scenes.title: The pomegranate and the journey
scenes.summary: Persephone rejoices; Hades secretly gives her a pomegranate seed. Hermes drives her to Demeter's temple and they embrace.
scenes.stakes: Persephone could be bound to the underworld by the food she ate.

scenes.title: Demeter questions her daughter
scenes.summary: Demeter fears a trick and asks whether Persephone ate; if so she must spend a third of each year below.
scenes.stakes: Whether Persephone can fully return to her mother.

scenes.title: Persephone tells her tale
scenes.summary: Persephone admits she was forced to taste the seed and recounts being seized while picking flowers with her companions.
scenes.stakes: Persephone's freedom, taken against her will.

characters.name: Demeter
characters.description: grieving goddess who withholds the harvest

characters.name: Hades

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet recalling Hermes' killing of the watchman Argus.
Another name for the lord of the dead.
Epithet for Hades, who receives all the dead.

notable_quotes.reason: Sets out the myth's explanation of the seasons, Persephone's third of the year below.

analysis.text: Eating the pomegranate seed binds Persephone to the underworld, and the compromise explains the cycle of seasons.
The hymn supports the Eleusinian Mysteries, whose rites promised a better fate after death.

legacy.text: The pomegranate-seed myth became the classic ancient explanation for the seasons and inspired countless later artworks and poems.

fun_facts.text: The list of Persephone's playmates names many Oceanids, and one, Pluto, shares a name with a god of the underworld.

language_notes.text: "So wrath was she" means she was so angry; "set foot on" Olympus means return there.
"Slayer of Argus" is an epithet of Hermes, who killed the hundred-eyed giant Argus; "Erebus" here means the dark underworld.
"Shy mate" means modest wife; "much reluctant" means she was very unwilling, being unhappy in the underworld.
"She" is Demeter, far away; "fell design" means a terrible plan, her scheme to withhold the crops.
Aidoneus is another name for Hades; "behest" means command.
"No unfitting husband" is understatement: Hades says he is a suitable husband, being Zeus's own brother.
Aidoneus is a poetic form of Hades; "Ruler of Many" is an epithet alluding to the multitude of the dead.
"Slayer of Argos" is an epithet of Hermes, recalling his killing of the hundred-eyed giant Argos.
"Clave" is an archaic past tense of "cleave": the horses split the air as they went.
"Her heart suddenly misgave her for some snare" means she suddenly suspected a trick.
"A third part of the seasons" means a third of each year spent below, the myth explaining winter.
"Rapt" means seized and carried off; "Host of Many" is another epithet of Hades, who receives all the dead.

context_notes.text: Hermes was the gods' messenger and guide of souls, so he could travel between Olympus and the underworld.
Eleusis, near Athens, was the site of Demeter's temple and the Eleusinian Mysteries, which this hymn explains.
Hades promises Persephone queenship over the dead and honour from mortals, who must appease the underworld powers with rites.
Maenads were female followers of Dionysus who roamed the mountains in ecstatic frenzy, so the comparison conveys Demeter's wild haste.
In Greek belief, eating the food of the dead bound a person to the underworld; hence the pomegranate seed matters.
The companions are the Oceanids, daughters of Ocean, joined by goddesses Athena (Pallas) and Artemis; Styx is the river of the underworld.

literary_notes.text: Stock descriptions like "all-seeing", "loud-thunderer" and "whose wand is of gold" give the gods their fixed Homeric identities.
Hermes presents Demeter's anger as a threat to humanity and to the gods' honours, showing her power.
Hades's grim smile hints that he agrees to release Persephone while knowing he has a trick in store.
The secret seed hints that Persephone's return will be incomplete and prepares the seasonal separation.
Sea, rivers, glens and peaks cannot check the horses, stressing their divine speed.
Demeter's rush from the temple is likened to a Maenad descending a wooded mountain, showing frenzied emotion.
The long list of nymphs' names evokes an idyllic world of girls and flowers, heightening the contrast with the abduction.
